title: You Didn't Ship a Bug. You Just Wrote It for a Human. - Ravi Madabhushi, Scalekit

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is authentication, authorization, identity, fine-grained access control, and governance for AI agents acting on behalf of human principals. The talk applies broadly to any agent system connecting to external tools, and Scalekit provides auth infrastructure for software builders. A production incident motivates the analysis, followed by architectural design recommendations for agent auth. Assumes familiarity with OAuth concepts, service account authentication, and MCP servers. Single-speaker conference presentation at the AI Engineer channel. All cited evidence is directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Ravi Madabhushi presents on the architectural mismatch between human-focused infrastructure and agent workloads. He opens with a real incident: a 'last seen' timestamp in Scalekit's identity platform, designed for human-scale login frequency, was being updated 60 times faster when agents started hitting their APIs, causing unnecessary database write pressure. The fix was simple—batching updates at second-level granularity—but it triggered a deeper investigation into how authentication and authorization assumptions break under agent workloads. Ravi draws on his decade-plus in identity infrastructure at Freshworks, where systems served millions of human daily users and machine-accessed APIs. The critical distinction: APIs accessed by deterministic programs written by humans are inspectable and code-reviewable, whereas agents are non-deterministic and probabilistic—behavior today doesn't guarantee behavior tomorrow. He outlines two existing authentication patterns: (1) human-as-principal-and-actor with delegated API access, and (2) service accounts with their own identity. Both assume the authenticating entity is the acting entity, with permissions fixed at registration time. This worked because deterministic programs stay in their lane. Agents break this on multiple fronts: principal and actor diverge (agents act on behalf of users), many systems lack proper OAuth support so there's no 'on behalf of' principal tracking, and agents lack determinism. Current MCP servers exacerbate this by surfacing all available tools regardless of which user authorized the agent, leading to wrong tool selection and rogue actions. Ravi cites incidents of agents deleting production databases. He argues for agent-bound principal identity, extremely fine-grained scoping at attribute, context, and principal levels, time-limited credentials tied to specific jobs, least-privilege-by-default, and just-in-time authorization for elevated scopes. He references ref.tools as a customer that built proper OAuth scoping for coding agents with no human actors. He emphasizes absolute visibility—every action must trace who took it, on behalf of whom, who authorized it, when, what authorization, and for how long. In closing, he stresses that teams who architected for humans and APIs must rethink their approach to provide deterministic guardrails and authorization controls for agents. OAuth is a good starting point, but agents require something beyond OAuth to ensure extremely fine-grained access controls, since agents always act independently on behalf of users.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: A 'last seen' timestamp designed for human login frequency caused 60x more database writes than expected when agents hit the API, exposing a fundamental human-centric design assumption.
The traditional principle that 'whoever authenticates is the one acting' breaks for agents because agents act on behalf of users, making principal and actor distinct entities.
Deterministic programs written by humans stay in their lane and can be code-reviewed; agents are non-deterministic and probabilistic, so past behavior doesn't guarantee future behavior.
Current OAuth scopes are too coarse—e.g., 'can send emails on your behalf' lacks time, sender, recipient, and context constraints needed for agent guardrails.
MCP servers typically surface all tools a user can access regardless of which user authorized the agent, leading to wrong tool selection and rogue actions.
Agents should be least-privileged by default with just-in-time authorization for elevated scopes, scoped at attribute, context, and principal levels with time limits tied to specific jobs.
Full audit visibility is non-negotiable: every action must trace who, on-behalf-of-whom, who authorized, when, what scope, and duration.

OAuth is a good starting point but insufficient alone—agents require deterministic guardrails and authorization controls beyond what OAuth provides, given they always act independently on behalf of users.

sections.title: Introduction and the Last-Seen Timestamp Incident
sections.summary: Ravi introduces himself and the talk's thesis: human-focused architecture doesn't scale for agents. He describes discovering rhythmic 15-minute latency spikes caused by a 'last seen' timestamp being updated 60x faster than designed when agents hit their APIs, straining DB writes. The quick fix was batching updates at second-level granularity, but it triggered deeper questions about auth assumptions.

sections.title: Background and the Fundamental Shift
sections.summary: Ravi shares his 10-year background in identity at Freshworks serving millions of human users. He explains that APIs accessed by machines written by humans were manageable, but the fundamental picture changed in the last 3-4 years. He observes that most agents customers build have far more permissions and scopes than their job requires, because existing primitives don't support fine-grained agent permissions.

sections.title: Two Existing Authentication Slots
sections.summary: Ravi outlines two existing auth patterns: (1) human authenticates and acts through their own application/script with an API key, and (2) service accounts with their own identity. Both share the philosophy that whoever authenticates is the one acting, with permissions fixed at registration time. This worked because deterministic programs stay in their lane and can be code-reviewed.

sections.title: How Agents Break the Determinism Assumption
sections.summary: Agents fundamentally break the existing assumption. The principal is not the same as the actor—agents need delegated access to act on behalf of users. Many systems still don't support OAuth, so there's no on-behalf-of principal. Critically, agents are non-deterministic: behavior today doesn't guarantee behavior tomorrow or even in the next run.

sections.title: MCP Server Tool Surfacing and Fine-Grained Scoping Needs
sections.summary: Most MCP servers surface all tools regardless of which user authorized the agent, letting agents pick wrong tools and do wrong things. Ravi argues agents need their own identity, bound to principals at all times, with extremely fine-grained scoping at attribute, context, and principal levels. Gmail's 'can send emails on your behalf' scope illustrates the coarseness problem—no time, sender, or recipient constraints.

sections.title: Least Privilege, Just-in-Time Auth, and the ref.tools Example
sections.summary: Agents should be least-privileged by default with just-in-time authorization for elevated scopes. Ravi cites ref.tools as a customer that built proper OAuth scoping for coding agents with no human actors, emphasizing this is a today problem. Agents have already caused incidents like deleting production databases.

sections.title: Visibility and Deterministic Control: Praying Is Not a Strategy
sections.summary: Ravi closes by stressing absolute visibility into every agent action: who took it, on behalf of whom, who authorized it, when, what authorization, and for how long. Without deterministic control over what agents can and cannot do, teams are merely hoping agents behave—and praying is not a strategy.

sections.title: Conclusion: Beyond OAuth for Agent Access Control
sections.summary: Ravi gives his final call to action: teams who architected for humans and APIs must rethink their approach to give agents deterministic guardrails and deterministic authorization controls. OAuth is a good starting point, but agents require something beyond OAuth to ensure extremely fine-grained access controls, since agents always act independently on behalf of certain users.
